Spring Boot follows a layered architecture in which
each layer communicates with the layer directly
below or above (hierarchical structure) it. The
four layers in Spring Boot are as follows:
- Presentation Layer: handles the HTTP requests,
translates the JSON parameter to object, and
authenticates the request and transfer it to the
- Business Layer: The business layer handles all
the business logic. It consists of service
classes and uses services provided by data
access layers. It also performs authorization
contains all the storage logic and translates
business objects from and to database rows.
- Database Layer: In the database layer, CRUD
* Role: The core annotation that tells Spring "this is the start of
my application." It triggers component scanning (to find your
classes) and auto-configuration. You saw this in your
* Role: Instead of manually creating objects (e.g., UserService
service = new UserService();), you let Spring create and manage
them for you. You simply ask for what you need, and Spring
* Role: Objects that are managed by the Spring IoC container. Any
* Controller (@RestController): Handles incoming HTTP requests and
* Service (@Service): Contains your business logic. Controllers
should be thin; they should delegate work here.
* Repository (@Repository): Handles data access. Your UserRepository
interface is a prime example—it extends JPA interfaces to perform
SQL operations without writing actual queries.
* Role: Java classes that map directly to database tables. Your
User.java and Post.java define the structure of your database.
